section.title: Zach Wilson: Job Hopping to Staff at Airbnb, Interviews, and Internal Brand
section.deck: Zach Wilson recounts a rapid climb from junior data engineer to staff at Airbnb, arguing that interviews and impact stories outpaced promotions, and counts the cost of long hours.

blocks.text: Zach Wilson describes a path from junior data engineer at Facebook (called Meta by the host) to staff data engineer at Airbnb by age 26. Zach's central argument is that the interview is the highest-leverage part of a career. Two of the level jumps came from changing companies, and in each case the tool was a clear impact story, not hours worked. Zach also lists the costs: roughly 60-hour weeks, a staff-type role taken before the matching behaviors were in place, and a Netflix reorganization that ended in a mental health break. The host adds that companies hold back promotions when someone has impact but not yet the behaviors. Pay figures and company details are Zach's recollection and are not verified.
blocks.heading: Interviews and impact stories move a career faster than waiting for a promotion

blocks.question: How did Zach get started in the industry?
answer: Zach began at several startups as a data analyst. A plan to become a math professor faded because it meant a lot of school for modest pay. An early job at Think Big Analytics taught Hadoop when it was new, about ten years before the recording, and Zach credits that experience as the main reason Facebook later wanted to hire.

Zach held four jobs in two years. On graduating, Zach was unsure whether to be a mobile engineer, a math professor or a data scientist, and tried several roles before settling on data engineering. With a dual major in computer science and applied math and only math tutoring on the resume, Zach still got four or five interviews and calls this luck.

followups.question: How did the Facebook offer come about, and why did Zach turn down a counter-offer?
answer: After a year in Utah, Zach moved to Washington, DC, to try something new. Six or seven months later a Facebook recruiter reached out on LinkedIn, a site Zach says has been critical since the Think Big job in 2015. Zach had been rejected twice by Google for mobile roles, so the approach felt almost as if Facebook were applying to Zach.

The DC employer countered. Zach recalls about 180 from Facebook against about 200 from the DC company, with units not stated. Zach declined because a request for a 20 percent raise two months earlier had been refused for lack of budget. Money that appears only when someone is leaving, Zach reasoned, signals that growth there would be painful.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: What was boot camp like, and how did Zach choose a team?
answer: Moving to Silicon Valley also put Zach closer to family in Utah, which had felt distant from DC. Zach says the first month of boot camp felt like Disneyland more than a job. The onboarding sold the company's values, such as moving fast and being bold, and felt like college because no deadlines applied yet.

Zach interviewed for three teams: ads, growth and community support. Ads pitched making Facebook millions through data, community support pitched preventing bad content, and growth pitched having fun. Zach joined core growth and notifications, partly on that pitch and partly because of an entrepreneurial manager who is still a close friend.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: Did Zach understand the career ladder on joining?
answer: No. Zach did not know what L3, L4 and L5 meant and did not realize the hire was at L3. Zach had two years of big-data pipeline work at startups, yet new Stanford graduates with no experience were paid the same, and Zach found that unfair. Zach concluded the hire was at the wrong level and worked hard to reach the next level, which took about seven months.
Zach says this taught that how someone interviews is the highest-leverage part of a career, more important than the impact made in the role.

followups.question: What did Zach do to earn the L3 to L4 promotion?
answer: Zach could tell early that things were going well: work was clearly tasked out, energy was high and a lot of code shipped. Notifications had a waterfall framework for tracking conversion, click and delivery rates, and Zach found it poor. Fixing it meant XHP and React work, not SQL and Python, so Zach learned both. Zach says the manager took this as proof of someone who solves problems outside the job description, and nobody had asked for it.
Doing only the assigned tasks, Zach says, earns a meets-all rating at L3, so Zach looked for where the impact was.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: Was the promotion expected?
answer: It came as a surprise. The half lasted five months for Zach because the start date was late July. Zach thinks the company recognized the mis-leveling and skipped the usual steps. The host adds that a promotion within one half usually signals a hiring miss that the company fixes quickly.

Zach contrasts this with Utah, where promotion follows tenure, not impact. In Utah, Zach had thought a software engineer would top out near 200k at about age 35. Facebook offered about that figure at the start, with a route toward a million, and Zach says companies reward business impact because the value created exceeds the pay.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: How many hours did Zach work at Facebook?
answer: After boot camp, Zach ramped up to roughly 50 to 60 hours a week, usually arriving around 9:30 and leaving near 8 pm, because breakfast, lunch and dinner were all provided. Zach jokes that free meals left a basic life skill, cooking, unlearned.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: After L4, why did the next promotion, to L5, not happen?
answer: Zach wanted L5 within a year and felt confident while the first manager was in place. That manager left the next summer. The team reported to the director for a while and then to a new manager from Netflix, so Zach had three managers in one year. None had the full context, and Zach had to restate past work again and again. Zach says this disrupted the plan, and that trust takes time to build. Zach says good managers extend trust by default, while others demand proof first.

Zach earned a greatly-exceeds rating in the first half as an L4 and again in the next. The feedback was that Zach was not yet operating as a senior engineer. Zach was taking on too much work, and leadership doubted that delivery at L5 level was sustainable.

followups.question: The host says a promotion must be sustainable, and a leader may wonder whether someone working long hours can keep it up. Did that match what Zach learned?
answer: Zach says it did, and calls it one of the most important lessons from Facebook. Hours worked do not necessarily drive promotion. Extra hours can cover a skill gap, but they do not give leadership confidence that someone is ready for the next level.
The host agrees that promotion committees look for behaviors, meaning the ability to take on more leadership, and not simply extra hours. The host notes this can leave a hard worker bitter.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: What did Zach do once the promotion stalled?
answer: Promotions at Facebook usually landed around March, and after learning there would be none, Zach decided it was time to take the story to market. Facebook had rated Zach as greatly exceeding expectations, which made it a strong story.

Zach points out that an interviewer does not see hours worked, only what was done, and gets a different vantage point on impact without much of the negative data from the current job. After the notification machine-learning optimizations and other technical work, Zach was sure a senior role was available at any big tech company by describing that work in detail.

followups.question: How did Zach sell a senior (IC5-level) profile at Netflix while still mid-level with few years of experience?
answer: Zach credits luck: the Netflix hiring manager was the former Facebook manager, who had already seen the work and trusted it. Zach says this is why building a network matters.

Zach separates personal brand, such as LinkedIn posts or videos, from internal brand, meaning how colleagues know a person. Zach says a strong internal brand was what worked here, built by working hard with that manager.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: What else, besides the stalled promotion, pushed Zach to leave Facebook? (editorial prompt for Zach's unprompted continuation)
answer: Zach also wanted to stop being a data engineer. On a team of about 15 data engineers, Zach says they wrote roughly 90 percent of the team's JavaScript. Zach also says data engineers sit off the engineering track and receive 30 to 40 percent less equity, a claim not verified here. Zach asked to switch to software engineering and was told it would mean a down-level to L3, which Zach rejected as absurd given what had already shipped. Zach says the title counted for more than the work, and that a manager who listens to career goals matters a great deal.

Zach adds that down-leveling when moving from data to software engineering was standard practice, but not the reverse. Zach also wanted bigger-data work, not just SQL, and says the role held at Facebook would be called analytics engineering today.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: Would a better manager have avoided the down-level?
answer: Zach believes so. A friend at Facebook whose manager was supportive made the transition this week, has been there about nine years, and lives, in Zach's words, the life Zach would have had with a better manager.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: How did the Netflix hire work, and how much did the old manager's backing count?
answer: The former manager said he could not hire Zach as a senior software engineer, given thin software experience, but could hire Zach as a senior data engineer and move Zach into software engineering within six to twelve months. After about six months Zach became a senior software engineer.

Zach recalls that in 2018 Netflix hired only seniors, with levels added about two years before the recording and no staff level. Managers controlled hiring, in line with the freedom-and-responsibility culture, and were also pressed to fire people. Zach contrasts this with Meta's standardized interviews, where a referral counts for less. Zach adds that this part of the culture has downsides.

The host reads this as an internal brand story: the manager had seen Zach deliver as a junior and wanted Zach on the team regardless of level. Zach agrees it matters more than people think, and says not to burn bridges and to find people you click with, since you may work with them again.

followups.question: What did the move do to pay?
answer: Zach says compensation roughly doubled to about 385 to 390, all of it cash. The captions garble the starting figure and give no units, so the numbers are approximate.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: What was Zach's plan at Netflix, and how did promotions and reviews work there?
answer: At 24, Zach pictured becoming a principal engineer (L7 or L8) by 30, doing deep technical work, and judged that data engineering would not get there. The Netflix work was real-time security threat detection, which Zach calls cutting-edge and hard.

Netflix had no promotions in the Meta sense. Managers gave a quarterly color: green meant fine, yellow meant pick it up, and red meant imminent firing. Once a year came a pay discussion based on what other companies would offer, not on past work, and a manager could adjust pay at any time.

Zach did not mind the lack of levels. Zach expected high pay and still had much to learn from the manager. Zach says to think about the story of impact at every company and to tell it in an exciting way.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: What does Zach mean by a story, and how does it support job hopping?
answer: Zach tends to leave jobs about every two years, so Zach has to be satisfied with the story first. At Airbnb, Zach felt an urge to quit early but realized there was no good story yet and stayed six more months. A story is a fully delivered package of impact that can be sold: if hired, here is what will be delivered in two years.

followups.question: What was the Facebook story that Zach sold to Netflix?
answer: Zach names three items. The first was a reachability metric for notifications, a counterweight to spam that tracked who was turning off settings and proved more complex than expected. The second was the first growth dashboard that covered WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger and Facebook in one chart. The third was the pipeline behind Facebook's notification-selection machine-learning algorithm, which Zach made 90 percent cheaper, or ten times more efficient, using sorted merge bucket joins.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: How does a job hopper handle the concern about short tenure?
answer: Zach says short tenure invites the thought that the person does not play well with others or is a disloyal job hopper. Zach says this must be defeated early in the interview, by showing ambition, hard problems solved and a path toward solving more. Zach has seen interviewers start skeptical and then warm up after a conversation.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: What made Zach leave Netflix?
answer: Zach says the first manager believed in Zach too much. Zach was on security threat detection when a separate team's asset-inventory role opened after a ten-year engineer left. Zach says it was a staff spot, not a senior one, and took it. Zach went from working with one team to interfacing with 11, was not ready for the volume of conversations, kept answering everyone and overworked. Netflix rewarded the move with a raise from the upper 300s to 550 the next year, by Zach's account.

In 2019 Netflix decided data engineering was no longer a necessary organization and folded it into data science. Zach says the VP, the director and the first manager were fired, and everyone began reporting to data science leaders.

followups.question: How did Zach respond to the reorganization?
answer: It caused so much stress that Zach took a month-long mental health break. Zach did not want to sit in a data science organization, having disliked that at Facebook, and wanted an engineering organization. Zach asked to transfer to the cyber security team, where the asset-inventory work belonged, and was told to stay in the current role.
Zach quit with nothing lined up, planning to travel the world in 2020. The last day was March 6, 2020, and COVID ended the plan. Zach says Netflix would pay a lot but give nothing else Zach wanted.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: What lesson did Zach take from that?
answer: Zach holds that a career should involve learning, earning or both, and that learning is better than earning, which is why Zach is now an entrepreneur. Zach says boredom at Airbnb came from the same cause: the pay was great, but Zach was not learning.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: The host says companies hold back promotions when someone has the impact but not the behaviors. What did Zach learn from being put in a staff role early?
answer: Zach agrees that the Netflix case shows the problem the delay is meant to prevent. Zach lists better work boundaries, planning ahead (a lesson Zach is relearning as an entrepreneur), and selling a technical vision. Zach says content creation has helped with the last one, which means presenting an idea so others will back it.

At earlier levels an engineer simply delivers the assigned work and solves the hard problem. At staff level, Zach says, the new behavior is deciding which problem to solve, which Zach found overwhelming at Netflix.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: How did Zach go from leaving Netflix to interviewing at Airbnb?
answer: By December 2020, Zach had played a lot of video games and felt unfulfilled and depressed. Zach's girlfriend at the time asked what Zach was doing with life, and they broke up. With no job, no partner and a dog to support, Zach decided to take another swing at interviewing.

Zach also started making content on LinkedIn that month, having told Netflix colleagues in March that they would see Zach again as a famous person. Zach regrets not starting during the pandemic, when growth was easier. Zach interviewed at Meta, Google and Airbnb, for software engineering at the first two and data engineering at Airbnb, and received offers from all three.

followups.question: How did the offers compare?
answer: Google and Facebook both offered senior roles. Zach recalls about 400 to 415 from Facebook and a lower Google figure that the captions cut off, similar to what Netflix had paid years earlier. Airbnb offered, by Zach's account, more than $100,000 above that, which made the choice easy even though the offers were not really competing.

Zach also liked how Airbnb does data engineering. The work was about 95 percent Scala and 5 percent Python, with no SQL, and the pipelines had to match online pricing and availability systems. Zach says this blend of pipelines, integrations and optimization was what Zach had wanted at Netflix.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: How did Zach get staff-level consideration with six years of experience when the posting asked for ten or more?
answer: Zach says Airbnb said the interview itself would decide between senior and staff. Zach credits the impact story from Netflix, including interfacing with 11 teams and solving a range of security problems. Zach also credits Netflix's feedback culture. Immediate, blunt feedback feels harsh at first, but Zach learned that colleagues wanted growth, and says Airbnb interviewers were impressed by that.

followups.question: Did Zach push for staff?
answer: Yes. The recruiter said up front that the result would be senior or staff, which annoyed Zach, who would not take a senior-only offer. Zach told the recruiter about the Facebook and Google interviews and said that if all three came in at senior, Zach would not pick Airbnb and would probably return to Facebook. Airbnb then leaned toward an interview-based middle path. Google and Facebook said they would offer senior only.
Zach's lesson is to interview at more than one company you are excited about, which lets you say what you need and walk away otherwise.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: Did the gap in years of experience matter?
answer: Zach had six years against a posting that asked for ten or more, and still got the offer. Zach's viral LinkedIn post on this had one message: apply for jobs you do not think you are ready for. Zach agrees that negotiating and selling made the difference.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: Some people may wonder whether Zach underperformed in the staff role. How did it go compared with Netflix?
answer: Zach thinks the Netflix difficulty came from two changes at once: a move from data to software engineering about a year earlier, and a jump into a staff-level leadership role. Zach had about one year of professional software engineering and says weekend side projects kept that from going badly. Together, the new job and the higher title raised burnout risk.

At Airbnb the staff role was in data engineering, where Zach felt confident. Leadership was present and the learning felt manageable. Zach says to change only one variable at a time. Zach was nervous about repeating the Netflix experience, but the Airbnb role turned out much calmer.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: How did the first year at Airbnb go?
answer: Zach got exceeds in the first half. Zach upgraded many pricing pipelines and wrote designs, which was higher-level work. The feedback was that Zach was close to greatly exceeds, and the gap was architecture. Airbnb wanted companywide work, while Zach wanted to stay on marketplace. They asked Zach to design best practices for moving data from the data lake back into production systems, the less straightforward direction, and Zach had no desire to do it.

In September 2021, Zach had a moment of clarity and asked whether to want promotion at all. Zach told the manager the work would not be done, though the manager said it was the work that would lead to the next level. Zach says it simply meant too many meetings.

followups.question: Did Zach's vision of becoming a principal engineer change?
answer: Zach says it did. Airbnb was handing over the path, but Zach was gaining traction on LinkedIn at about 50,000 followers and now cared about other things. Zach told the manager the job would still get done, and aimed to put Airbnb on a coasting footing by doing the bare minimum.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: Zach had strong managers earlier. How did Zach build an internal brand at Airbnb from zero?
answer: Zach tries, in each new job, to do something in three months that makes people say this person is something else. At Airbnb it was the pricing and availability pipeline, which computes prices and availability daily and was among the messiest pipelines Zach had seen. Zach was assigned to move it onto the paved road, Airbnb's approach for building high-quality, platform-compatible pipelines, with a year-end target. Zach finished in the first quarter, and the pipeline then stopped running late and ran smoothly.

Zach says the signal is twofold: the person ramped up fast and also landed big impact fast. It also showed Zach could manage risk, since pricing is vital to Airbnb and Zach followed best practices carefully. Zach looks for systems that everyone knows could be better but nobody touches because the work is risky, complex or painful.

followups.question: Did Zach know in advance that the work would have impact?
answer: No, it was handed over. Three months into a job, Zach says, everything is handed over, and it takes at least six months to develop an internal compass of the company. Zach sees it as a trade-off, and the aim was to build a brand early.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: How did colleagues react?
answer: Zach says people do not trust a new hire and some actively distrust one. Some senior engineers disliked Zach for being hired at staff, since they had worked four years for that promotion and assumed the level was simply handed to an external hire. Zach also thinks the senior-to-staff promotion is unnecessarily difficult at most companies.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.label: Host's reading: interview versus promotion
blocks.text: The host says the interview shows its value here: Zach landed the level with less than six months of work, while colleagues went through hoops for years. The host adds an analogy to pre-revenue startups, which get generous offers because the outcome is open, and says a track record builds inertia: an employer that hired someone at one level resists moving them up. In the host's view the interview has more variance, so it gives a step change while promotion inside a company gives only a gradual one. This is the host's analysis, not Zach's.

blocks.question: How many hours did Zach work at Airbnb?
answer: Zach says Airbnb was far better in 2021, at about 40 hours a week and perhaps a little more, compared with about 60 at Facebook and Netflix. Zach had assumed that exceeds was impossible without long hours and had expected a meets rating, and says that being happy with meets was fine as long as there was no firing.
blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.label: Host's reading: hours at staff level
blocks.text: The host has met people afraid of a staff promotion because they think it locks them into much more than 40 hours a week, and reads Zach's case as proof that in at least some cases it does not. In the host's view the shift is toward identifying high-leverage opportunities, which is not necessarily grind. The host adds that it can feel grindy for some people at staff, and that sometimes such opportunities are simply not there. This is the host's view, not Zach's.

blocks.question: What about Zach's personality helped across this career?
answer: Zach names three traits. The first is a tenacious willingness to keep learning. Even while working about 60 hours a week at Facebook, Zach founded a startup and spent weekends on it, to learn JavaScript and full-stack development. Zach says that was critical to this year's success as an entrepreneur, since the platform is JavaScript-based.

The second is positivity and visible enthusiasm. Showing up excited is contagious, makes others like their jobs more and like Zach, and leads to opportunities. Zach adds that a manager's job is largely to get people to like their jobs.
The third is refusing to tolerate what feels unfair, and changing life instead of enduring it. Zach calls this a double-edged sword that is not always good.

followups.question: Would staying at Meta have produced a similar path?
answer: Zach thinks a similar trajectory was possible by staying and finding a better manager, and would have been less chaotic. Zach says the many health plans and 401(k)s to merge across jobs were a hassle. The host replies that staying would still have meant being dissatisfied and switching teams, which carries risk, and that Zach's first trait explains why the first manager trusted Zach so much.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.question: If Zach started again as an IC3, what would Zach change?
answer: Zach would be more open to other perspectives. In the first years Zach focused on becoming the most technical person, and now thinks that matters mostly up to senior engineer. After that, technical skill helps only marginally and other skills are needed.

Zach did not start building soft skills until Netflix, when things were on fire and the skills were urgently needed. Developing them earlier at Facebook, in lower-risk situations where failure felt smaller, would have given better balance and probably faster growth.

Zach also says not to eat dinner at work. Zach calls it a scam: in Zach's view, Facebook and Google offer it to keep people at the office longer. Zach would have used those hours for the gym, since fitness started only in 2018, and for other parts of life.

followups.question: Given the fast growth, does Zach wish for less work, and was it worth it?
answer: Zach says the growth was worth it, and Zach now aims for balance and tranquility. Zach would not repeat the work from age 22 to 25, but does not regret it, because it was what Zach needed to feel powerful and grow. Zach adds that health matters: earning $20 million while stressed and dying at 50 is not a good life, and health, wealth and happiness each matter differently at different times.

Zach also says working hard gave a young person a sense of purpose by making them useful. Zach then asks whether that purpose could have come without so many sleepless nights, nights of feeling out of depth, and a couple of panic attacks. Zach says such costs are rarely discussed.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

followups.question: The host sums up the advice to an IC3-level Zach. What does Zach add?
answer: The host sums up the advice as: stop being one-dimensional, keep working hard, look after health and enjoy the ride. Zach agrees on enjoying the ride more and not becoming fixated on getting promoted, and says things come in time for those who put in the hours daily. Zach believes the universe gives people what they want if they are willing to pay the price.
followups.speaker: Zach Wilson

blocks.speaker: Zach Wilson
